# Glossary {-}

Each term is defined at first use in the body text. This is the lookup table,
not the definition of record. Symbols are collected separately in Appendix
\@ref(notation).

**Ambient dimension**
: The dimension $D$ of the space the data are *observed* in, as distinct from
  the intrinsic dimension of the manifold they lie on. A folded sheet is
  observed in $\mathbb{R}^3$ and can be lifted to any larger $D$ without its
  intrinsic dimension changing.

**Autoencoder**
: A network trained to reconstruct its own input through a narrow bottleneck.
  Encoder maps to the bottleneck, decoder maps back. The only method here that
  learns an explicit inverse rather than a one-way map.

**Classical multidimensional scaling (MDS)**
: Embedding by eigendecomposition of the doubly centred matrix of squared
  distances. Equivalent to PCA when the distances are Euclidean; the two part
  company only once they are not.

**Continuity ($C_k$)**
: Rank-based metric penalising *missed* neighbours — points close together in
  the ambient data that the embedding pulls apart. The complement of
  trustworthiness.

**Crease pattern**
: The planar graph of fold lines drawn on the flat sheet, together with a
  mountain/valley assignment. Here it doubles as the ground-truth embedding.

**Developable surface**
: A surface that can be flattened into a plane without stretching or tearing.

**Diffusion map**
: Embedding by the eigenvectors of a Markov transition matrix built on a
  kernel-weighted neighbourhood graph. Embedded distance approximates diffusion
  distance — how differently two starting points spread after $t$ steps.

**Embedding**
: A map from the ambient sample to lower-dimensional coordinates, and by
  extension the $n \times q$ matrix $Y$ it produces. Whether the map is an
  embedding in the topological sense is precisely what the benchmark tests.

**Facet**
: A flat polygonal region of a crease pattern, bounded by creases and by the
  edge of the sheet. Rigid folding moves facets without deforming them.

**Flat-foldability**
: The property that a pattern can be folded flat — every facet parallel to one
  plane — without the sheet passing through itself. Maekawa's and Kawasaki's
  theorems are necessary conditions at a single vertex; satisfying them at every
  vertex is not sufficient for the pattern as a whole.

**Fold angle ($\theta$)**
: The dihedral angle at a crease. Runs from 0 (flat sheet) to $\theta_{\max}$
  (fully compressed) and serves as the difficulty parameter throughout.

**Gaussian curvature**
: The product of the two principal curvatures. It is intrinsic, so isometries
  preserve it. A folded sheet has zero Gaussian curvature everywhere: on facets
  by flatness, and at each interior vertex because the sector angles around it
  still sum to $2\pi$. Folding cannot create curvature, only hide flatness.

**Geodesic distance**
: The length of the shortest path between two points measured *along* a surface
  rather than through the space around it. Unchanged by folding, which is the
  premise the book rests on.

**Huzita–Hatori axioms**
: Seven operations describing what a single fold can construct by aligning given
  points and lines. Strictly stronger than compass and straightedge — they solve
  cubics, and so trisect an angle and double the cube. Background; nothing in
  the benchmark depends on them.

**Interior vertex**
: A vertex of a crease pattern not lying on the boundary of the sheet.
  Maekawa's and Kawasaki's conditions constrain interior vertices only.

**Intrinsic dimension**
: The number of coordinates needed to parameterise a manifold locally,
  independent of the space it sits in. Written $d$; two for a single crease
  pattern, $2k$ for a $k$-factor product.

**Isomap**
: Classical MDS applied to geodesic distances estimated as shortest paths
  through a kNN graph. Built for exactly the isometric case constructed here,
  which is why the informative result is where it breaks rather than where it
  works.

**Isometry**
: A map that preserves distances measured *along* the surface. Rigid folding is
  an isometry; this is the property the whole book rests on.

**Kawasaki's theorem**
: At a flat-foldable interior vertex the alternating sum of the sector angles
  vanishes, $\beta_1 - \beta_2 + \cdots - \beta_{2m} = 0$; equivalently the
  odd-indexed and even-indexed angles each sum to $\pi$.

**Kernel PCA**
: PCA performed on the Gram matrix of a kernel instead of the covariance of the
  data. Nonlinear in the input space while remaining a single eigenproblem. The
  bridge from linear projections into the geodesic methods.

**kNN graph**
: The graph joining each point to its $k$ nearest neighbours in ambient
  distance. Shared substrate of Isomap, LLE, Laplacian eigenmaps, UMAP and every
  rank-based metric used here — which is why those methods and those metrics
  tend to fail together rather than independently.

**kNN preservation ($P_k$)**
: The mean fraction of each point's $k$ ambient neighbours that survive as
  neighbours in the embedding. The most direct of the rank-based metrics, and
  the bluntest.

**Kruskal stress**
: A normalised sum of squared discrepancies between ambient and embedded
  distances, written $\sigma_1$. Zero for an exact isometric embedding. Computed
  here on raw distances, without the monotone regression step of non-metric MDS.

**Laplacian eigenmaps**
: Embedding by the eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian of a kNN graph, taken at
  the smallest non-zero eigenvalues. Preserves local proximity and says nothing
  about global scale.

**Latent space**
: The bottleneck coordinate system of an autoencoder — its learned analogue of
  the true unfolding. Nothing constrains the two to agree even up to similarity;
  checking whether they do is the point of Chapter \@ref(autoencoders).

**Lift**
: Multiplication by a matrix with orthonormal columns, carrying the ambient
  sample isometrically into a higher-dimensional space. Changes the ambient
  dimension and nothing else: the intrinsic geometry, and so the answer key, is
  untouched.

**Locally linear embedding (LLE)**
: Embedding that reconstructs each point as a weighted combination of its
  neighbours, then finds low-dimensional coordinates preserving those weights.
  Assumes every neighbourhood is approximately a linear patch — an assumption a
  crease violates by construction.

**Maekawa's theorem**
: At a flat-foldable interior vertex the numbers of mountain and valley creases
  differ by exactly two, $\lvert M \rvert - \lvert V \rvert = \pm 2$. The degree
  of such a vertex is therefore even.

**Manifold hypothesis**
: The assumption that high-dimensional data concentrate near a low-dimensional
  manifold. Manifold-learning theory usually adds a smoothness assumption on top
  of it. A crease pattern satisfies the hypothesis and violates the smoothness,
  which is the situation real data are also in.

**Miura-ori**
: The tessellation of congruent parallelogram facets in a zig-zag of mountain
  and valley creases, parameterised by $(a, b, \alpha)$ and folded by the single
  degree of freedom $\theta$. The default pattern family here.

**Mountain / valley assignment**
: The direction of each crease. Written M and V; encoded by linetype as well as
  colour in every figure.

**Perplexity**
: t-SNE's smooth measure of effective neighbourhood size, defined as $2^{H}$ for
  the Shannon entropy $H$ of the conditional neighbour distribution. Plays the
  role that $k$ plays elsewhere; UMAP's counterpart is `n_neighbors`.

**Principal component analysis (PCA)**
: Orthogonal projection onto the directions of greatest variance, computed here
  by singular value decomposition of the centred data. Exact at $\theta = 0$ and
  at no other fold angle.

**Procrustes alignment**
: The similarity transform — rotation or reflection $R$, scale $s$, translation
  $t$ — minimising squared distance between two configurations. Applied before
  any embedding is compared to the truth, because an embedding can only ever be
  correct up to similarity.

**Product manifold**
: The Cartesian product of $k$ folded patterns: intrinsic dimension $2k$ inside
  ambient $\mathbb{R}^{3k}$, with the answer key the product of the individual
  unfoldings. How the benchmark escapes intrinsic dimension two.

**Rigid origami**
: Folding in which facets stay flat and all deformation happens at creases.

**S-curve**
: A sheet bent into an S in $\mathbb{R}^3$. With the Swiss roll, one of the two
  standard synthetic benchmarks: one fixed geometry, everywhere smooth, no
  difficulty parameter.

**Seed variance**
: The spread of a metric across random seeds at one fixed configuration. The
  reference against which any between-method difference must be judged. A gap
  smaller than the seed variance is not a result.

**Short-circuit**
: Two points close in ambient space but far apart geodesically. The failure mode
  that breaks kNN-graph methods.

**Swiss roll**
: A plane rolled into a spiral in $\mathbb{R}^3$; the standard benchmark for
  nonlinear dimension reduction and the comparator in Chapter
  \@ref(comparison). It is genuinely isometric to a rectangle and so does have
  an answer key — but one fixed geometry, uniform curvature, and no knob to turn.

**t-SNE**
: Neighbour embedding that matches a Gaussian neighbour distribution in the
  ambient space against a heavy-tailed Student-$t$ one in the embedding, by
  minimising KL divergence. Preserves local structure; distances between
  clusters and the apparent size of clusters are not interpretable.

**Trustworthiness ($T_k$)**
: Rank-based metric penalising *false* neighbours — points the embedding places
  together that were far apart in the ambient data. The complement of
  continuity.

**UMAP**
: Neighbour embedding that builds a fuzzy simplicial set on the kNN graph and
  optimises a cross-entropy against its low-dimensional counterpart. Faster than
  t-SNE and generally more willing to preserve global arrangement; equally
  seed-dependent.

**Waterbomb**
: A tessellation built from the waterbomb base — a square creased along both
  diagonals and both midlines. Its degree-six vertices leave more than one
  degree of freedom, so folding it means choosing a one-parameter path through
  its configuration space rather than following the only one available.

**Yoshimura**
: The diamond tessellation that appears when a thin-walled cylinder buckles
  under axial compression. It folds a flat strip into a corrugated cylinder, so
  it is the one family here whose sheet can be closed on itself rather than left
  as a rectangle.
